pll1d16c2-d1e3477.summary: Notes that the Son, as made man, is said to be less not only than the Father but also than the Spirit and himself.
claims: As man the Son is less than the Father, the Spirit, and himself.

pll1d16c2-d1e3480.summary: With De Trinitate I: men erred by applying to his eternal substance what is said of Christ as man, like 'the Father is greater than I.' This is said because of the form of a servant, according to which he is less even than himself, having emptied himself without losing the form of God. In the form of God he is equal to the Father; in the form of a servant less, even than himself. Scripture rightly says both.
claims: What is said of Christ as man must not be applied to his divine substance.
In the form of God the Son is equal to the Father.
In the form of a servant the Son is less even than himself.

pll1d16c2-d1e3519.summary: Adds De Trinitate II and Augustine to Maximinus: in the form of a servant the Son is less than the Father, the Spirit, and himself, and made a little lower than the angels (Heb 2:9). He is equal to the Father by nature, less by habitus.
claims: The Son as man is less than the Father, the Spirit, and himself.
He was made a little lower than the angels.
He is equal by nature and less by habitus.

pll1d16c2-d1e3576.summary: Concludes from these authorities that according to the form of a servant the Son is less than the Father, himself, and the Spirit.
claims: As man the Son is less than the Father, himself, and the Spirit.

pll1d16c2-d1e3579.summary: Notes that Hilary seems to say the Father is greater than the Son, yet the Son is not less. The Father is greater by authority, as the one in whom the authority of generation lies, and this is the sense of 'the Father is greater than I,' like 'gave him a name above every name.' With De Trinitate IX: the Father is greater by the giver's authority, but the Son is not less, since what is given is to be one with him in the Father's glory. Lombard urges the reader to note Hilary's words wherever they occur and read them piously.
claims: The Father is greater by the authority of generation.
The Son is not less, since he is given to be one with the Father.
The Father gives the Son to be as great as himself.
Hilary's words should be read carefully and piously.

pl-l1d16c2.summary: Notes that, according to the form of a servant, the Son is less not only than the Father but also than the Spirit and himself. With Augustine, the error of applying to Christ's eternal substance what is said of his humanity ('the Father is greater than I') is avoided by distinguishing the form of God, in which he is equal, from the form of a servant, in which he is less even than himself, and lower than the angels: equal by nature, lesser by habitus. Hilary seems to say instead that the Father is greater by the authority of giving (generation) and yet the Son is not less, since what is given is to be one with the Father. Lombard urges that Hilary's words be read carefully and piously.
claims: According to the form of a servant the Son is less than the Father, the Spirit, and himself.
Christ's statements about his humanity must not be applied to his eternal substance.
In the form of God the Son is equal to the Father; in the form of a servant he is less.
The Son is equal to the Father by nature and less by habitus.
Hilary says the Father is greater by the authority of the giver, yet the Son is not less, since he is given to be one with the Father.
